sql_schemas: table leave_requests | fields: id, employee_id, leave_type, start_date, end_date, reason, status, approved_by, approved_at, created_at, updated_at | pk: id | fks: employee_id -> employees.id; approved_by -> employees.id | indexes: employee_id: high-frequency lookups — every employee views their own leave history; also used by manager team views; status: filtering by status (SUBMITTED for manager approval queues, APPROVED for calendar views) is the dominant access pattern; leave_type: filtering by leave type (annual/sick/emergency) for balance calculations and reporting; start_date, end_date: date-range queries for calendar views, overlap detection, and fiscal-year scoping; (employee_id, status): composite access pattern — 'show me my pending requests' is the most frequent employee query

table leave_balances | fields: id, employee_id, policy_id, total_entitlement, used_days, remaining_days, fiscal_year, status, created_at, updated_at | pk: id | fks: employee_id -> employees.id; policy_id -> leave_policies.id | indexes: employee_id: every balance check is scoped to an employee; the most frequent query; policy_id: joins to policy for entitlement rules during accrual calculations; fiscal_year: balance queries are always scoped to a fiscal year; used in WHERE clauses on every balance read; (employee_id, fiscal_year): composite key for the dominant access pattern — 'get this employee's balance for this year'; (employee_id, policy_id, fiscal_year): uniqueness enforcement — one balance row per employee per policy per fiscal year

table leave_policies | fields: id, policy_name, leave_type, entitlement_days, accrual_rate, max_accumulation, minimum_notice_days, requires_manager_approval, is_active, created_at, updated_at | pk: id | indexes: leave_type: filtering policies by leave type is the primary lookup — 'what policy applies to annual leave?'; is_active: active-policy filtering on every policy resolution query; (leave_type, is_active): composite for the dominant access pattern — 'get the active policy for sick leave'

table audit_logs | fields: id, entity_type, entity_id, action, old_values, new_values, performed_by, performed_at, created_at | pk: id | fks: performed_by -> employees.id | indexes: entity_type, entity_id: every audit lookup is scoped to a specific entity — 'show me the change history for leave request X'; performed_by: audit reports filtered by actor — 'what actions did manager Y take?'; performed_at: time-range queries for audit reports and compliance exports; action: filtering by action type (APPROVE, REJECT) for approval audit trails; (entity_type, entity_id, performed_at): composite for the dominant access pattern — chronological change history for a specific entity

table employees | fields: id, employee_number, first_name, last_name, email, manager_id, department, hire_date, termination_date, employment_status, created_at, updated_at, deleted_at | pk: id | fks: manager_id -> employees.id | indexes: employee_number: unique lookup by employee number — used in HR imports and payroll integration; email: unique lookup for authentication and notification delivery; manager_id: manager-team queries — 'get all direct reports for manager X' — used in approval workflows; department: departmental filtering for HR reports and team calendars; employment_status: filtering active employees for leave eligibility checks

data_notes: Persistence slice for the leave management module. Five conceptual tables defined: leave_requests (core entity with status lifecycle), leave_balances (per employee/policy/fiscal-year with composite uniqueness), leave_policies (leave type configuration), audit_logs (GP-002 compliance for all state-changing operations), and employees (referenced by FK relationships). Four repository interfaces with concrete Pg* implementations backed by PostgreSQL via pg Pool (src/shared/db/connection.ts). Index rationale reflects dominant access patterns: employee-scoped lookups, status filtering for approval queues, date-range queries for calendar views, and composite indexes for the most frequent query shapes. The audit_logs table satisfies GP-002 — every state change (create, approve, reject, update, cancel) writes an immutable audit record with actor, timestamp, old/new values, and entity reference.
